summary: The change does what was asked. `athena drain` now writes a pid file (drain.pid) holding its pid, a process start marker and its build, and removes it when it ends. A second live drain is refused, and a drain whose build is older than the landed code refuses to start and dispatches nothing. The new commands drain-status, drain-stop --wait and drain-restart find the drain only through that file and never match command text or send signals. drain-restart rebuilds with ./setup.sh, waits for the old drain to exit, rebuilds again if that drain landed code meanwhile, starts the new drain in the background and prints the build it runs. A failed rebuild starts nothing. I ran each planned test and all passed; they use real child processes, including decoys whose command lines contain 'drain'. I also ran drain-status and drain-restart --help through the binary in this snapshot. fmt, clippy and the full test suite passed in Athena's recorded CI run, which I did not repeat. CHANGELOG and README describe the commands, the root cause and the one-time transition for drains started before the pid file existed, and label the 5% figure an estimate. All six changed files are on the deliverables list. Findings are minor: restart's first rebuild can overlap a rebuild the old drain is doing for its own landing, and the macOS ps path is tested only through its parser. One nit: drain-status --json has no help text.
